text_blocks.snippet: To control high blood sugar, several types of medications are available, including oral and injectable options, each working through different mechanisms to lower glucose levels. Common oral medications include metformin, sulfonylureas, meglitinides, thiazolidinediones, DPP-4 inhibitors, and alpha-glucosidase inhibitors. Injectable medications include GLP-1 receptor agonists (often administered via injection) and insulin.
snippet_highlighted_words: metformin, sulfonylureas, meglitinides, thiazolidinediones, DPP-4 inhibitors, and alpha-glucosidase inhibitors

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed look at some of these medications:

list.title: Metformin:
list.snippet: A commonly prescribed medication, metformin reduces glucose production in the liver and makes the body more responsive to insulin.

list.title: Sulfonylureas:
list.snippet: These drugs, such as glipizide, glimepiride, and glyburide, stimulate the pancreas to release more insulin.

list.title: Meglitinides:
list.snippet: Medications like repaglinide and nateglinide help lower blood sugar after meals by stimulating insulin release.

list.title: Thiazolidinediones:
list.snippet: Pioglitazone and rosiglitazone improve insulin sensitivity in muscle and fat tissue and reduce glucose production in the liver.

list.title: DPP-4 Inhibitors:
list.snippet: Medications like sitagliptin and saxagliptin prevent the breakdown of GLP-1, a hormone that helps lower blood sugar, and can also increase feelings of fullness.

list.title: Alpha-Glucosidase Inhibitors:
list.snippet: Acarbose and miglitol slow down the digestion and absorption of carbohydrates, which helps reduce post-meal blood sugar spikes.

list.title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists:
list.snippet: These medications, including dulaglutide, exenatide, liraglutide, and semaglutide, are injected and help lower blood sugar by slowing digestion and increasing insulin release. Some GLP-1 agonists may also reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke.

list.title: Insulin:
list.snippet: Insulin therapy is often necessary for individuals with type 1 diabetes and may be required for some with type 2 diabetes.

list.title: SGLT2 inhibitors:
list.snippet: Medications like canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin help the kidneys remove excess sugar through urine.

list.title: Dopamine-2 agonists:
list.snippet: Bromocriptine is a medication that can help treat type 2 diabetes by resetting the body's natural circadian rhythm, which can improve insulin resistance and reduce glucose production.

list.title: Individualized Treatment:
list.snippet: It's crucial to work with a healthcare professional to determine the most appropriate medication or combination of medications based on individual needs, health conditions, and lifestyle.
